description_full: CSW Industrials, Inc. provides various industrial products in the Americas, Europe, the Middle East and Africa, and the Asia Pacific regions. The Contractor Solutions segment offers condensate pads, pans, and pumps; condensate switches and traps; drain management system; drain waste and vent systems mechanical products; ductless mini-split systems installation support tools and accessories; HVAC electrical protection, installation supplies, and maintenance chemicals; evaporator coils and air handlers; grilles, registers, and diffusers and vents; line set covers; load management systems; motors and capacitors; refrigerant caps; solvents, cements, traps, and thread sealants; surge protections; and wire pulling head tools under the Amrad, AquaGuard, Aspen Manufacturing, Clean Check, Cover Guard, Desolv, Duckt-Strip, Dust Free, EZ Trap, Falcon, Fortress, Goliath, G-O-N, Guardian Drain Lock, Hubsett, Kickstart, Leak Freeze, MARS, No. 5, Novent, PF WaterWorks, PRO-Fit, PSP Products, RectorSeal, Safe-T-Switch, Shoemaker Manufacturing, SureSeal, TRU-BLU, TRUaire, and Turbo 200 brands. The Engineered Building Solutions segment offers architectural railings and metals; expansion joints and joint seals; fire and smoke curtains, and fire stopping solutions; perimeter protection; and pre-engineered and custom architectural building components under the Balco, BlazeSeal, Duraspan, Greco, IllumiTread, Jointspan, Metacaulk, Metablock, Metaflex, Quakespan, and Smoke Guard brands. The Specialized Reliability Solutions segment provides compounds, lubricants, and sealants; industrial maintenance and repair, anti-seize, contamination control, and desiccant breather filtration; lubricant management systems; operation solutions; andrail applicators, and friction modifiers under the AccuTrack, OilSafe, Air Sentry, BioRail, Deacon, Envirolube, Extreme, Gearmate, Hydrotex, Jet-Lube, Kopr-Kote, Matrix, and Whitmore brands. The company was incorporated in 2014 and is based in Dallas, Texas.

financial_summary: CSW Industrials, Inc. is a mid-cap industrials business with a $4.4B market cap on $1.1B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +13% over the past three years and +13% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 15% against a 9% cost of capital, a 6-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, with gross margins sitting at 44%.

The business throws off $132M in free cash flow — roughly 12 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.34× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 4.5× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and interest coverage runs at 8.1×.
Shareholder yield of 3.4% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 4.0% of the shares.

sect: Its 16% operating margin runs 7pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.41x).
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+14.4% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 544 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 19% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 20% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 24% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 44% and a beta of 1.00, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.86 vs 5y 0.99), so read it loosely.
About $36.2M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 27% in the 2020 crash and 22% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $174 (margin of safety -56%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 36%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $119 to $251 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Industrials peers: P/E 34.9 vs 23.3, EV/EBITDA 17.1 vs 13.3 and P/FCF 33.4 vs 22.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 6% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.0% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.2% (vs the 8% bar).
The 7 covering analysts target $343 on average, 26% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 15% earns above the cost of capital of 8.7%, but the 6pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.37).
It runs a 44% gross margin and converts 12% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is mixed: cash conversion of 1.34x, but a weak Piotroski score of 3/9.
ROE of 11% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.2x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.5% of revenue on R&D.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 4.5x net debt to EBITDA ($33.8M of cash against $869.3M of debt), with interest covered 8.1x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 3.5, in the safe zone).
Working capital ties up about 206 days of sales, a drag on cash generation.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 12.6% over 3 years, 20.9% over 5 years and 13.0% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 14%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 18.2% a year over five years.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.1x, 1.6% of sales), a maintenance pace.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 5.4% on average.
Analysts expect 9.0% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own a modest 4.0%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only sold over the past year (7 sales, net $4.0M sold).
It returns 3.4% a year to shareholders (3.0% in buybacks and 0.4% in dividends).
The share count has grown 0.6% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
people: With about 2,700 employees, each generates about $401K of revenue, in line with the Industrials median, and productivity has risen 13.0% a year.
That works out to $49K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.3M (6x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
